prompt: Kubernetes 1.24 removed its built-in support for the Docker Engine. Why did images built with `docker build` keep running on it?
hint: What kind of image does `docker build` produce?

choices.text: They are OCI images, which containerd and CRI-O run
choices.why: Right. The format is standard; the engine was never what the cluster needed.

choices.text: Kubernetes quietly converts each Docker image into its own format at pull time
choices.why: No conversion happens; the image is already in the standard format.

choices.text: Docker images contain a copy of the Docker Engine
choices.why: An image holds the program's files, not an engine.

choices.text: Clusters kept Docker installed on every node for compatibility
choices.why: 1.24 removed exactly that path; clusters talk to containerd or CRI-O.

choices.text: It was written by the Kubernetes project
choices.why: Kubernetes uses runtimes; runc came from elsewhere.

choices.text: It is part of the Linux kernel
choices.why: It is an ordinary program that asks the kernel for namespaces and cgroups.

choices.text: Docker gave its container-starting code to the OCI
choices.why: Right, when the OCI was founded under the Linux Foundation.

choices.text: Podman's authors wrote it to replace Docker's engine
choices.why: Podman came later and uses runc or crun as its runtime.

prompt: `docker info --format "{{.DefaultRuntime}}"` printed the name of the program that finally creates the container's process: ___.
How does the same name, `alpine:3.22`, give a Raspberry Pi and an `amd64` server each the right binaries?
hint: Open the document the index points to.

choices.text: The registry looks at the client's IP address
choices.why: Registries do not guess; the client chooses.

choices.text: The tag's index lists each platform
choices.why: Right. That list had eight platforms.

choices.text: Alpine's binaries run on any processor
choices.why: Lesson 2 showed an arm64 binary refused on amd64.

choices.text: There are separate tags, and Docker silently rewrites the name
choices.why: One tag, one index, many manifests; nothing is renamed.

prompt: The manifest names the layer `sha256:53f8…`, and the configuration's `rootfs.diff_ids` says `sha256:e477…`. Why two hashes for one layer?

choices.text: One is a hash of the compressed archive, the other of the files uncompressed
choices.why: Right. The manifest names what travels; `diff_ids` names what it unpacks to.

choices.text: The layer was changed after the image was published, and the configuration was never updated to match it
choices.why: Any change would break the manifest's digest; both hashes are correct for different things.

choices.text: One uses SHA-256 and the other SHA-512
choices.why: Both are written `sha256:`.

choices.text: The second belongs to the arm64 variant
choices.why: Both are in the amd64 image's own documents.

prompt: Somebody appends one byte to a layer stored in a registry. What happens when Ana pulls the image?
hint: The blob's name is the hash of its bytes.

choices.text: Nothing visible; one byte is too small to matter
choices.why: Any byte changes the hash completely, as the tampered copy showed.

choices.text: The pull fails on the digest
choices.why: Right: the bytes no longer match the digest the manifest names. Content addressing makes the change detectable.

choices.text: Docker repairs the layer from the arm64 variant
choices.why: Other platforms hold other binaries; nothing repairs a layer.

choices.text: The tag `3.22` moves to the changed image automatically
choices.why: The manifest still names the original digest, which the bytes no longer match.

prompt: Why does `docker run -it alpine:3.22`, with no command, open a shell?

choices.text: Docker opens a shell for any image
choices.why: `postgres:17` started PostgreSQL in lesson 1; the default comes from each image.

choices.text: Alpine has no other program
choices.why: The layer lists 519 entries, many of them programs.

choices.text: Because `-it` means "interactive shell"
choices.why: `-it` keeps input open and allocates a terminal; it chooses no program.

choices.text: Its config says `Cmd` is `/bin/sh`
choices.why: Right. The image's configuration carries the default command.

prompt: What can a digest promise that a tag like `3.22` cannot?

choices.text: That the image is free of vulnerabilities
choices.why: A digest identifies content; it says nothing about its quality. Lesson 20.

choices.text: That it names one exact image forever
choices.why: Right. Change a byte and the digest changes; a tag can be moved to another image.

choices.text: That the image is the newest release
choices.why: Nothing about a digest says new or old.

choices.text: That the image runs on any platform
choices.why: A platform manifest's digest names the image for one platform.

prompt: What does runc need in a bundle to start a container? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A root filesystem directory
choices.why: Yes: `rootfs`, unpacked from the image.

choices.text: A `config.json` describing the process
choices.why: Yes: written by `runc spec` and edited by Ana.

choices.text: A running Docker daemon
choices.why: Ana started the bundle with no Docker involved.

choices.text: A registry to pull from
choices.why: runc only reads a directory; pulling is Docker's job.

prompt: Ana started the bundle as herself, yet `ps` inside reported the user as `root`. What explains it?

choices.text: runc runs everything as root on the host, whoever starts it
choices.why: Ana used no `sudo`; the process belongs to her outside.

choices.text: A user namespace maps her account to root inside
choices.why: Right. Inside it is UID 0; outside, still Ana.

choices.text: Alpine has no other users
choices.why: Alpine's `/etc/passwd` lists several; the mapping decides who she is.

choices.text: `ps` in Alpine always prints `root`, whatever the user
choices.why: It printed `root` because inside, the process is UID 0.

prompt: Ana's rootless `config.json` lists pid, ipc, uts, mount and user namespaces. Which consequence follows?

choices.text: The container cannot see its own files
choices.why: The mount namespace and `rootfs` give it its own files.

choices.text: It would share Ana's network, since there is no network namespace
choices.why: Right. Without that wall, it sees the host's interfaces.

choices.text: It cannot set its host name
choices.why: The `uts` namespace is there, and it printed `runc`.

choices.text: It sees the host's processes, because it shares the host's process table
choices.why: The `pid` namespace is there; `ps` showed one process.

prompt: Which of these does Docker do that runc alone does not? Choose all that apply.
hint: runc starts a process from a directory.

choices.text: Pull images from a registry
choices.why: Yes. runc has no idea what a registry is.

choices.text: Put the process in namespaces
choices.why: That is runc's job; it did it for Ana with no Docker.

choices.text: Keep a record of containers and their logs
choices.why: Yes. runc forgets a container when it exits.

choices.text: Publish ports and create networks
choices.why: Yes. runc starts a process; the networking around it is Docker's.

prompt: An image is copied byte for byte from Docker Hub to a cloud provider's registry. What happens to its digest?
hint: What is the digest computed from?

choices.text: It changes to the new registry's format
choices.why: The format is the same OCI format on both.

choices.text: It is prefixed with the provider's name
choices.why: The name of the repository changes; the digest is a hash of the bytes.

choices.text: It stays the same
choices.why: Right: the bytes are the same, so the hash is the same. That is what makes the registry interchangeable.

choices.text: It becomes invalid until the image is rebuilt
choices.why: Nothing needs rebuilding; identical bytes give an identical hash.

prompt: In alpine's image index, half the entries say `unknown/unknown`. What are they?

choices.text: Platforms Docker does not support yet
choices.why: They are not platforms at all.

choices.text: Broken manifests the registry should delete
choices.why: They are deliberate and belong with the images.

choices.text: Attestations about how each image was built
choices.why: Right. Lesson 20 reads them.

choices.text: Images for Windows, which Linux reports as unknown
choices.why: Alpine publishes no Windows image; these are attestations.
